source.note: 英文逐字稿取自 YouTube 字幕；中文為學習用翻譯。版權屬原作者，僅供個人學習。

title: This Science-Backed Morning Routine Will REPROGRAM Your Mind!

lines.en: Hey everyone, welcome back to On Purpose.
lines.zh: 大家好，歡迎回到 On Purpose。

lines.en: Today is about how to reprogram your mind before 8:00 a.m.
lines.zh: 今天要談的是如何在早上 8 點前重新設定你的大腦。

lines.en: I want to share with you the most practical science-backed morning routine that I could find and I actually tried myself.
lines.zh: 我想和你分享我能找到、而且自己也實際試過，最實用、有科學根據的晨間作息。

lines.en: Here's something nobody tells you about your morning.
lines.zh: 有一件關於早晨的事，沒有人會告訴你。

lines.en: The first 60 to 90 minutes after you open your eyes is neurologically speaking the most programmable window of your entire day.
lines.zh: 從神經科學的角度來說，睜開眼睛後的頭 60 到 90 分鐘，是你一整天中最容易被「設定」的時段。

lines.en: Your brain is literally in a different state.
lines.zh: 你的大腦真的處在不同的狀態。

lines.en: It's transitioning out of theta and alpha brainwave patterns, the same frequencies used in hypnotherapy, into the waking beta state you'll spend the rest of your day in.
lines.zh: 它正從 θ 波和 α 波的腦波模式，也就是催眠治療使用的相同頻率，轉換到你接下來一整天都會處在的清醒 β 波狀態。

lines.en: And what do most of us do with that window? We hand it over.
lines.zh: 而我們大多數人怎麼使用這段時間？我們把它拱手讓人。

lines.en: We pick up our phone, we scroll through someone else's priorities, someone else's outrage, someone else's curated highlight reel.
lines.zh: 我們拿起手機，滑過別人的優先事項、別人的憤怒、別人精挑細選的精彩片段。

lines.en: And we wonder why we feel behind before the day has even started.
lines.zh: 然後納悶為什麼一天還沒開始，就覺得自己已經落後了。

lines.en: Today, I want to share the most practical, simple, genuinely achievable morning routine I found.
lines.zh: 今天我想分享我找到最實用、最簡單、真正做得到的晨間作息。

lines.en: One that I tried myself.
lines.zh: 一套我自己試過的作息。

lines.en: One built entirely on neuroscience and peer-reviewed research.
lines.zh: 完全建立在神經科學和經過同儕審查的研究上。

lines.en: And I promise you, there's no ice baths at 4:00 a.m., no 2-hour rituals that require monastic training, just six small,
lines.zh: 我保證沒有凌晨 4 點的冰浴，沒有需要修道院訓練的兩小時儀式，只有六個小小的、

lines.en: surprising, science-backed steps that take about 45 minutes total and that anyone, night owls included, can start tomorrow.
lines.zh: 令人意外又有科學根據的步驟，總共大約 45 分鐘，任何人，包括夜貓子，明天就能開始。

lines.en: And here's what I love about each one.
lines.zh: 而我喜歡每一個步驟的地方在於：

lines.en: There's a clear reason why it works at a biological level.
lines.zh: 它們在生物層面上都有明確的原理。

lines.en: When you understand the mechanism, you're not relying on motivation.
lines.zh: 當你了解背後的機制，你就不用靠意志力。

lines.en: You're working with your brain, not against it. Let's get into it.
lines.zh: 你是順著大腦運作，而不是和它作對。我們開始吧。

lines.en: I know mornings are something we all struggle with and I want to be honest, I've struggled with them as well.
lines.zh: 我知道早晨是我們都會掙扎的時段，老實說，我也一樣。

lines.en: It's not easy for me to wake up energized and early.
lines.zh: 要我精神飽滿地早起並不容易。

lines.en: Sometimes I want to stay in bed.
lines.zh: 有時候我想賴床。

lines.en: Sometimes I want to scroll too and end up doing that as well.
lines.zh: 有時候我也想滑手機，結果也真的滑了。

lines.en: And so I've worked really hard on developing some of these habits that have changed the way I feel.
lines.zh: 所以我很努力地培養其中一些習慣，它們改變了我的感受。

lines.en: I want you to go through your day feeling ready, energized, and prepared, and I found that when we do certain things, we actually end up doing the opposite.
lines.zh: 我希望你一整天都覺得準備好了、精力充沛，而我發現當我們做某些事時，結果其實會適得其反。

lines.en: So, let's start with the most controversial thing I'm going to say today.
lines.zh: 那我們就從今天我要說的最具爭議性的一件事開始。

lines.en: Hitting the snooze button is one of the worst things you can do for your brain in the morning. Here's why.
lines.zh: 按下貪睡鈕是你早上對大腦能做的最糟的事之一。原因如下。

lines.en: When your alarm goes off, your brain is finishing its final sleep cycle, usually REM sleep, the phase critical for memory consolidation and emotional processing.
lines.zh: 鬧鐘響的時候，你的大腦正在完成最後一個睡眠週期，通常是快速動眼期，這是鞏固記憶和處理情緒的關鍵階段。

lines.en: When you hit snooze and drift off for another 9 minutes or nine times, your brain starts a brand new sleep cycle that it cannot possibly finish.
lines.zh: 當你按下貪睡、再睡個 9 分鐘或按個九次，大腦就會開始一個全新的、根本不可能完成的睡眠週期。

lines.en: You're essentially fragmenting your sleep into useless chunks.
lines.zh: 你基本上是把睡眠切成一塊一塊沒用的碎片。

lines.en: Research on sleep inertia, that's the scientific term for that groggy, disoriented fog you feel after waking, shows that fragmented sleep from snoozing actually worsens cognitive function.
lines.zh: 關於「睡眠慣性」，也就是醒來後那種昏沉、迷糊的科學說法，研究顯示按貪睡造成的片段睡眠，其實會讓認知功能變差。

lines.en: We're talking about slower reaction times, impaired memory, and reduced executive function.
lines.zh: 我們說的是反應變慢、記憶受損、執行功能下降。

lines.en: You're not getting rest in those extra minutes. You're creating neurological confusion.
lines.zh: 那多出來的幾分鐘你並沒有得到休息，而是在製造神經上的混亂。

lines.en: The internal clock, controlled by a tiny brain region, gets conflicting signals, and the grogginess can linger for hours.
lines.zh: 由大腦一個小區域控制的生理時鐘會收到矛盾的訊號，那種昏沉感可能持續好幾個小時。

lines.en: So, what do you do instead?
lines.zh: 那該怎麼做呢？

lines.en: I'm going to share something with you.
lines.zh: 我要跟你分享一件事。

lines.en: It's a little weird, but I want you to try it.
lines.zh: 有點怪，但我希望你試試看。

lines.en: I want you to try something called the future you is calling alarm.
lines.zh: 我希望你試一種叫「未來的你打來了」的鬧鐘。

lines.en: Now, I've never loved the word alarm because we think about alarms as a fire alarm, when there's an alert, when there's some danger.
lines.zh: 我一直都不太喜歡「警報（alarm）」這個字，因為我們會聯想到火災警報、有危險時的警告。

lines.en: Imagine you're actually shocking yourself to wake up out of danger.
lines.zh: 想像一下，你其實是在嚇自己，好從危險中醒來。

lines.en: But, try the future you is calling.
lines.zh: 但試試「未來的你打來了」。

lines.en: Before bed, record a 10- to 15-second voice memo pretending you're you from 6 months in the future.
lines.zh: 睡前錄一段 10 到 15 秒的語音備忘錄，假裝你是六個月後的自己。

lines.en: It could even be that morning.
lines.zh: 甚至可以是那天早上的自己。

lines.en: Not motivational fluff, make it oddly specific and slightly dramatic.
lines.zh: 不要空洞的勵志話，要講得具體得有點奇怪，還要帶點戲劇性。

lines.en: For example, "Hey, it's you.
lines.zh: 例如：「嘿，是我。

lines.en: I'm literally standing in the kitchen of the life you wanted. Don't hit snooze.
lines.zh: 我正站在你想要的那種生活的廚房裡。不要按貪睡。

lines.en: Today is one of the days that got me here.
lines.zh: 今天就是讓我走到這裡的其中一天。

lines.en: Also, you still hate rushed mornings, right?" That's just an example.
lines.zh: 還有，你還是很討厭匆匆忙忙的早晨，對吧？」這只是一個例子。

lines.en: Set that recording as your alarm.
lines.zh: 把那段錄音設成你的鬧鐘。

lines.en: And here's why this works.
lines.zh: 這方法為什麼有效？

lines.en: Your brain doesn't expect your own voice. It breaks the autopilot.
lines.zh: 你的大腦不會預期聽到自己的聲音，這會打破自動駕駛模式。

lines.en: Future you creates curiosity instead of dread.
lines.zh: 未來的你會引起好奇，而不是恐懼。

lines.en: It reframes waking up as time travel, not obligation.
lines.zh: 它把起床重新定義成時光旅行，而不是義務。

lines.en: And you could put your phone outside your bedroom and only allow yourself to hear the ending of the message if you stand up and walk to it.
lines.zh: 你也可以把手機放在臥室外面，只有站起來走過去，才能聽到訊息的結尾。

lines.en: What I find fascinating about this example is that we're completely tricking the brain. Right?
lines.zh: 我覺得這個例子很有意思的地方是，我們完全是在騙過大腦，對吧？

lines.en: Usually, you think we have to force ourselves out of bed.
lines.zh: 通常你會覺得我們得強迫自己下床。

lines.en: Usually, we have to find a way to get that energy.
lines.zh: 通常我們得想辦法擠出那股能量。

lines.en: When you hear your own voice in the morning that says, "It would mean so much for us to wake up right now."
lines.zh: 當你早上聽到自己的聲音說：「現在起床對我們來說意義重大。」

lines.en: Because if we wake up right now, we'll actually be really happy. Because guess what?
lines.zh: 因為如果我們現在起床，就會真的很開心。因為你猜怎樣？

lines.en: There's a voice in your head telling you, "Go to sleep. Go to sleep. Go to sleep."
lines.zh: 你腦中有個聲音一直說：「去睡、去睡、去睡。」

lines.en: And we're not strong enough to fight it in our head.
lines.zh: 而我們在腦中不夠強大，贏不了它。

lines.en: And that's why the alarm does that for you. Right?
lines.zh: 所以鬧鐘替你做這件事，對吧？

lines.en: Having an alarm that's your voice telling you the reasons you want to wake up, the amazing day you want to have,
lines.zh: 用你自己的聲音當鬧鐘，告訴你想起床的理由、你想過的美好一天、

lines.en: the life you want to build to encourage you specifically is actually allowing you to externalize that powerful voice, that motivated voice, that conscious voice before the subconscious takes over.
lines.zh: 你想打造的人生，專門為你打氣，這其實是在潛意識接管之前，把那個強大、有動力、有意識的聲音放到外面來。

lines.en: The subconscious is saying, "Just lie in. Hit the snooze button. Sleep in more. It doesn't matter.
lines.zh: 潛意識會說：「再躺一下吧。按貪睡鈕。多睡一點。沒關係的。

lines.en: It won't make a difference."
lines.zh: 不會有什麼差別。」

lines.en: And your conscious mind at that time is switched off.
lines.zh: 而你的意識在那個時候是關機的。

lines.en: It doesn't have the ability to fight back.
lines.zh: 它沒有能力反擊。

lines.en: So, use your conscious mind to create a conscious alarm.
lines.zh: 所以用你的意識來設定一個有意識的鬧鐘。

lines.en: I also want you to seriously consider moving your alarm across the room if you need to.
lines.zh: 如果需要的話，我也希望你認真考慮把鬧鐘放到房間另一頭。

lines.en: The physical act of standing upright triggers a blood pressure change that signals wakefulness to your brain.
lines.zh: 站起來這個動作會引發血壓變化，向大腦發出清醒的訊號。

lines.en: But the voice note alarm is key.
lines.zh: 但語音備忘錄鬧鐘才是關鍵。

lines.en: It's a micro decision that becomes a macro habit. Step number two.
lines.zh: 這是一個會變成大習慣的小決定。第二步。

lines.en: Now you want sunlight in your eyes, the free drug.
lines.zh: 現在你要讓陽光照進眼睛，這是免費的藥。

lines.en: This might be the single most impactful thing on the entire list and it costs you absolutely nothing.
lines.zh: 這可能是整張清單上影響最大的一件事，而且完全不用花錢。

lines.en: Within the first 30 to 60 minutes of waking up, get outside and expose your eyes to natural sunlight for 10 to 20 minutes.
lines.zh: 起床後的 30 到 60 分鐘內，到戶外讓眼睛接觸自然陽光 10 到 20 分鐘。

lines.en: Now I know that sounds like a long time.
lines.zh: 我知道這聽起來很久。

lines.en: You could have your morning coffee, you could do a small workout outside, you could pace and take a phone call if you wanted to.
lines.zh: 你可以喝早晨的咖啡、在戶外做點小運動，或是邊走邊講電話。

lines.en: Not through a window ideally, not through sunglasses.
lines.zh: 最好不要隔著窗戶，也不要戴太陽眼鏡。

lines.en: Outside with the light hitting your retinas.
lines.zh: 要在戶外，讓光照到你的視網膜。

lines.en: Here's the science and it's genuinely fascinating.
lines.zh: 科學原理是這樣，而且真的很有意思。

lines.en: Your eyes contain specialized cells called intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells or ipRGCs if that makes it any easier, that have almost nothing to do with vision.
lines.zh: 你的眼睛裡有一種特殊的細胞，叫做「本質感光視網膜神經節細胞」，簡稱 ipRGC 可能比較好記，它們幾乎和視覺無關。

lines.en: Their job is to detect ambient light and send timing signals directly to the part of the brain that's the master clock I mentioned earlier.
lines.zh: 它們的工作是偵測環境光線，並把時間訊號直接傳到大腦中我剛才提到的主時鐘。

lines.en: That signal does several things simultaneously.
lines.zh: 那個訊號會同時做好幾件事。

lines.en: First, it triggers a healthy pulse of cortisol.
lines.zh: 第一，它會觸發一次健康的皮質醇分泌。

lines.en: Now before you panic, cortisol gets a bad reputation as the stress hormone, but the morning cortisol awakening response is not the same thing as chronic stress cortisol.
lines.zh: 在你慌張之前，皮質醇因為被稱為「壓力荷爾蒙」而名聲不好，但早晨的皮質醇覺醒反應，和慢性壓力的皮質醇不是同一回事。

lines.en: Research published in multiple peer-reviewed journals shows that this natural morning surge, which peaks about 30 to 45 minutes after waking,
lines.zh: 發表在多份同儕審查期刊的研究顯示，這種自然的早晨高峰，大約在起床後 30 到 45 分鐘達到頂點，

lines.en: promotes alertness, supports immune function, and sets the emotional baseline for your entire day.
lines.zh: 它能提升警覺、支持免疫功能，並為你一整天的情緒定下基調。

lines.en: About 77% of healthy people experience this response, and light exposure amplifies it in the right direction.
lines.zh: 大約 77% 的健康人會有這種反應，而光照會把它往對的方向放大。

lines.en: Second, that same light signal tells your pineal gland to start the 14-hour countdown to melatonin production.
lines.zh: 第二，同樣的光訊號會告訴你的松果體開始 14 小時倒數，準備分泌褪黑激素。

lines.en: That means morning sunlight doesn't just help you wake up, it directly programs better sleep tonight.
lines.zh: 也就是說，早晨的陽光不只幫你醒來，還直接讓你今晚睡得更好。

lines.en: It's a 24-hour investment disguised as a 15-minute walk.
lines.zh: 這是偽裝成 15 分鐘散步的 24 小時投資。

lines.en: Third, and this one surprised me, research on office workers found that those who got significantly more bright light exposure before noon scored substantially higher on cognitive performance tests after just 5 days. 5 days.
lines.zh: 第三，這點讓我很驚訝，一項針對上班族的研究發現，中午前接觸明顯更多亮光的人，短短 5 天後的認知表現測驗分數就大幅提高。5 天。

lines.en: And separate work from Northwestern University found that people who got the majority of their light exposure earlier in the day had lower body weight compared to those who got light later.
lines.zh: 而西北大學另一項研究發現，大部分光照集中在一天較早時段的人，體重比晚一點才照光的人低。

lines.en: So, here's the practical step.
lines.zh: 所以實際步驟是這樣。

lines.en: Walk outside for 10 to 20 minutes after waking.
lines.zh: 起床後到戶外走 10 到 20 分鐘。

lines.en: Combine it with your coffee, your dog walk, or just standing on your porch.
lines.zh: 可以結合喝咖啡、遛狗，或只是站在門廊上。

lines.en: On overcast days, you're still getting significantly more lux.
lines.zh: 陰天時，你得到的勒克斯還是明顯多得多。

lines.en: That's the unit of light intensity than any indoor light provides.
lines.zh: 勒克斯是光照強度的單位，比任何室內燈光提供的都多。

lines.en: If it's pitch dark when you wake up, use a 10,000 lux light therapy lamp positioned at eye level for 20 to 30 minutes, and skip the sunglasses during the window.
lines.zh: 如果你起床時外面還一片漆黑，就用一盞一萬勒克斯的光療燈，放在與眼睛同高的位置照 20 到 30 分鐘，這段時間不要戴太陽眼鏡。

lines.en: Regular glasses and contacts are fine, but your eyes need that full spectrum light input.
lines.zh: 一般眼鏡和隱形眼鏡沒問題，但你的眼睛需要全光譜的光線輸入。

lines.en: Obviously, don't stare directly at the sun just to point it out.
lines.zh: 當然，順帶一提，不要為了這個直視太陽。

lines.en: But light exposure is huge.
lines.zh: 但光照真的很重要。

lines.en: It's it's helping you sleep better, it's helping you wake better, it's helping you have better energy.
lines.zh: 它幫你睡得更好、醒得更好、精力更好。

lines.en: And here, I know what you're saying, Jay, how do I get 10 to 20 minutes? I get it.
lines.zh: 我知道你在想什麼：Jay，我哪來 10 到 20 分鐘？我懂。

lines.en: Even if you can start with 1 or 2.
lines.zh: 就算從 1、2 分鐘開始也好。

lines.en: If you can start with 1 or 2 minutes, it will make a huge difference in your life, and I hope you'll give it a go.
lines.zh: 如果能從 1、2 分鐘開始，對你的生活就會有很大的不同，希望你試試看。

lines.en: Step number three, the 90-second cold shock.
lines.zh: 第三步，90 秒冷水衝擊。

lines.en: I promise you no 4:00 a.m. ice baths, but stay with me.
lines.zh: 我保證沒有凌晨 4 點的冰浴，但先聽我說。

lines.en: Before you skip ahead, I'm not going to tell you to take a 20-minute ice bath.
lines.zh: 在你跳過之前，我不會叫你泡 20 分鐘冰浴。

lines.en: I'm going to tell you to do something much simpler, and honestly, much more interesting from a neuroscience perspective.
lines.zh: 我要你做的事簡單得多，而且老實說，從神經科學的角度來看有趣得多。

lines.en: At the end of your normal shower, turn the water to cold for 60 to 90 seconds. That's it.
lines.zh: 平常洗澡洗到最後，把水轉成冷水 60 到 90 秒。就這樣。

lines.en: Here's what happens in your body during those 60 to 90 seconds.
lines.zh: 這 60 到 90 秒裡，你的身體會發生這些事。

lines.en: Cold water activates your sympathetic nervous system, the fight-or-flight response, which triggers a rapid release of norepinephrine and adrenaline.
lines.zh: 冷水會啟動交感神經系統，也就是「戰或逃」反應，觸發正腎上腺素和腎上腺素快速釋放。

lines.en: These are the same neurotransmitters responsible for alertness, attention, and mood elevation.
lines.zh: 這些就是負責警覺、專注和提振心情的神經傳導物質。

lines.en: It's essentially a natural stimulant.
lines.zh: 它基本上是一種天然的興奮劑。

lines.en: But the more interesting research is about what happens after the cold exposure.
lines.zh: 但更有趣的研究是關於冷水接觸之後發生的事。

lines.en: A study looking at cold water immersion found that cortisol levels and negative mood ratings were both measurably lower 3 hours after just 15 minutes of cold exposure.
lines.zh: 一項關於冷水浸泡的研究發現，接觸冷水 15 分鐘後，3 小時內皮質醇濃度和負面情緒評分都明顯降低。

lines.en: So, the initial shock wakes you up, but the downstream effect is actually a calmer, more resilient baseline for the rest of your morning.
lines.zh: 所以一開始的衝擊讓你清醒，但後續效果其實是讓你接下來整個早上的基礎狀態更平靜、更有韌性。

lines.en: And here's the really compelling finding.
lines.zh: 而這是非常有說服力的發現。

lines.en: Research on people who did regular cold exposure, just two to three times per week for 12 weeks, showed that their cortisol response to the cold dropped significantly after only 4 weeks.
lines.zh: 一項研究針對定期接觸冷水的人，每週只要兩到三次、持續 12 週，結果只過了 4 週，他們對冷水的皮質醇反應就明顯下降。

lines.en: Their bodies adapted. But critically, researchers believe this adaptation generalizes.
lines.zh: 他們的身體適應了。但關鍵是，研究人員認為這種適應會類化到其他地方。

lines.en: Meaning your body may also become better at managing cortisol responses to other stresses.
lines.zh: 也就是說，你的身體可能也會更擅長應付其他壓力引起的皮質醇反應。

lines.en: Work stress, relational stress, the daily chaos of life.
lines.zh: 工作壓力、人際壓力、日常生活的混亂。

lines.en: You're essentially training your nervous system to be less reactive.
lines.zh: 你基本上是在訓練你的神經系統變得不那麼容易起反應。

lines.en: There's also a neurological angle that fascinates me.
lines.zh: 還有一個讓我很著迷的神經學角度。

lines.en: Your skin has a significantly higher density of cold receptors than warm receptors, especially on your face, where you might have 10 or more cold sensing spots per square centimeter for every two warm sensing ones.
lines.zh: 你皮膚上的冷覺受器密度比溫覺受器高很多，尤其是臉上，每平方公分大約有 10 個以上的冷覺點，溫覺點只有兩個。

lines.en: Cold water on your face activates the vagus nerve through what's called the dive reflex, which shifts your nervous system toward the parasympathetic, the rest and digest mode.
lines.zh: 冷水潑在臉上會透過所謂的「潛水反射」啟動迷走神經，讓你的神經系統轉向副交感神經，也就是休息與消化模式。

lines.en: It's a reset button. Here's the practical step.
lines.zh: 它就像一個重置鍵。實際步驟是這樣。

lines.en: At the end of your regular warm shower, turn the dial to cold and stay in for just 60 to 90 seconds.
lines.zh: 平常溫水澡洗到最後，把水轉成冷水，只要撐 60 到 90 秒。

lines.en: Focus on breathing slowly and steadily through the discomfort.
lines.zh: 專注在不舒服中緩慢、平穩地呼吸。

lines.en: If a cold shower feels too extreme, start with just splashing cold water on your face and the back of your neck for 30 seconds.
lines.zh: 如果冷水澡感覺太極端，就先從用冷水潑臉和後頸 30 秒開始。

lines.en: Even that partial exposure activates the vagus nerve and triggers a norepinephrine response. Build up from there.
lines.zh: 即使只是部分接觸，也能啟動迷走神經並觸發正腎上腺素反應。再從那裡慢慢增加。

lines.en: The goal isn't to suffer.
lines.zh: 目標不是受苦。

lines.en: The goal is controlled brief discomfort that re-wires your stress tolerance.
lines.zh: 目標是可控制的短暫不適，重新建構你對壓力的耐受度。

lines.en: Now, I've been trying all of these out.
lines.zh: 我一直在試這些方法。

lines.en: The voice alarm in the morning worked incredibly well for me.
lines.zh: 早上的語音鬧鐘對我非常有效。

lines.en: The sunlight, I haven't been able to do 10 to 20 minutes, but even just doing the 1 to 2 minutes.
lines.zh: 陽光的部分，我一直沒辦法做到 10 到 20 分鐘，但就算只做 1 到 2 分鐘也有用。

lines.en: I did 10 to 20 minutes when I first tested this out for like 30 days, but my schedule's got busier, so I'm trying to do 1 to 2 minutes at least of direct sun exposure.
lines.zh: 我剛開始測試時大概 30 天都做了 10 到 20 分鐘，但後來行程變忙，所以我盡量至少直接曬 1 到 2 分鐘的太陽。

lines.en: And this one, the 60 to 90 seconds, is an absolute game-changer. These are all free.
lines.zh: 而這個 60 到 90 秒的冷水，絕對是改變遊戲規則的方法。這些全部都免費。

lines.en: You don't have to download an app.
lines.zh: 你不用下載任何 app。

lines.en: You don't have to learn anything new.
lines.zh: 你不用學任何新東西。

lines.en: Step number four, move for 7 minutes, not 60.
lines.zh: 第四步，動 7 分鐘就好，不用 60 分鐘。

lines.en: One of the biggest myths about morning routines is that you need a full gym session to get the neurochemical benefits of exercise.
lines.zh: 關於晨間作息最大的迷思之一，是你需要完整的健身課程才能得到運動帶來的神經化學好處。

lines.en: You don't, and the research proves it.
lines.zh: 你不需要，研究也證明了這一點。

lines.en: A study published by the American College of Sports Medicine validated what's now known as the 7-minute workout, a high-intensity circuit of 12 bodyweight exercises, 30 seconds each, with brief rest intervals.
lines.zh: 美國運動醫學會發表的一項研究，證實了現在所謂的「7 分鐘運動」：12 個徒手動作組成的高強度循環訓練，每個 30 秒，中間短暫休息。

lines.en: The findings showed that this short burst of activity was sufficient to trigger meaningful cardiovascular and metabolic benefits comparable in several measures to much longer moderate-intensity sessions.
lines.zh: 研究結果顯示，這短短一段運動就足以帶來有意義的心血管和代謝益處，在好幾項指標上都和長得多的中等強度運動不相上下。

lines.en: But here's what I want you to focus on from a brain perspective.
lines.zh: 但從大腦的角度，我希望你注意這一點。

lines.en: When you move your body in the morning, you're not just burning calories.
lines.zh: 早上活動身體時，你不只是在燃燒熱量。

lines.en: You're doing four things neurologically.
lines.zh: 你在神經上做了四件事。

lines.en: One, you're increasing blood flow to the prefrontal cortex, the seat of decision-making, planning, and impulse control.
lines.zh: 第一，你增加了流向前額葉皮質的血流，那裡是做決定、規劃和控制衝動的中樞。

lines.en: This is the part of your brain that's slowest to come fully online after sleep, and movement accelerates that process.
lines.zh: 這是大腦睡醒後最慢完全上線的部分，而活動會加速這個過程。

lines.en: Two, you're triggering the release of BDNF, brain-derived neurotrophic factor, which is essentially fertilizer for your neurons.
lines.zh: 第二，你觸發了 BDNF，也就是腦源性神經營養因子的釋放，它基本上就是神經元的肥料。

lines.en: BDNF promotes the growth of new neural connections and strengthens existing ones.
lines.zh: BDNF 會促進新神經連結的生長，並強化既有的連結。

lines.en: It's one of the most important molecules for learning, memory, and cognitive flexibility.
lines.zh: 它是學習、記憶和認知彈性最重要的分子之一。

lines.en: Three, you're flooding your brain with endorphins, serotonin, and dopamine, the trifecta of mood-regulating transmitters.
lines.zh: 第三，你讓大腦充滿腦內啡、血清素和多巴胺，這是調節情緒的三大神經傳導物質。

lines.en: This isn't just feeling good.
lines.zh: 這不只是感覺很好而已。

lines.en: These chemicals directly affect your capacity for focus, motivation, and emotional regulation for hours afterward.
lines.zh: 這些化學物質會直接影響你接下來幾個小時的專注力、動力和情緒調節能力。

lines.en: And four, physical movement, especially if done outside, creates a state that neuroscientists call optic flow.
lines.zh: 第四，身體活動，尤其是在戶外，會產生一種神經科學家稱為「光流」的狀態。

lines.en: When you walk or run and the visual world streams past you, it activates circuits in your brain that reduce activity in the amygdala, your threat detection center.
lines.zh: 當你走路或跑步，視覺世界從你身邊流過，會啟動大腦中降低杏仁核活動的迴路，杏仁核就是你偵測威脅的中心。

lines.en: It's one of the reasons walking feels so calming.
lines.zh: 這就是走路讓人覺得很放鬆的原因之一。

lines.en: It's not just the exercise, it's the visual processing. Here's the practical step.
lines.zh: 不只是因為運動，還有視覺處理。實際步驟是這樣。

lines.en: Do 7 minutes of bodyweight movement.
lines.zh: 做 7 分鐘的徒手運動。

lines.en: Push-ups, squats, lunges, jumping jacks, anything that elevates your heart rate.
lines.zh: 伏地挺身、深蹲、弓箭步、開合跳，任何能讓心跳加速的都可以。

lines.en: If you want structure, search for the scientific 7-minute workout and it's free and widely available.
lines.zh: 如果你想要有架構，搜尋「科學 7 分鐘運動」，免費而且到處都找得到。

lines.en: If 7 minutes feels like too much, start with three.
lines.zh: 如果 7 分鐘感覺太多，就從 3 分鐘開始。

lines.en: Do it in your pajamas if you want.
lines.zh: 想穿睡衣做也可以。

lines.en: The barrier to entry should be almost zero.
lines.zh: 開始的門檻應該幾乎是零。

lines.en: You're not training for a marathon, you're telling your brain that the day has begun.
lines.zh: 你不是在練馬拉松，你只是在告訴大腦：一天開始了。

lines.en: I think for so long we've just put so much pressure on needing an entire workout.
lines.zh: 我覺得長久以來，我們都給自己太大壓力，覺得非得做完整的運動不可。

lines.en: And I know what you're thinking, Jay, what's 7 minutes going to do?
lines.zh: 我知道你在想：Jay，7 分鐘能有什麼用？

lines.en: Here's what it's going to do.
lines.zh: 它能做到的是這樣。

lines.en: It's going to give you the energy and the motivation to do 14 minutes, to do 30 minutes, to try and invest more time.
lines.zh: 它會給你能量和動力去做 14 分鐘、做 30 分鐘，試著投入更多時間。

lines.en: I think as humans we get into this perfectionist mentality. It's either all.
lines.zh: 我覺得人類很容易陷入完美主義的心態：要嘛全有，

lines.en: I'm either going to do an amazing workout or nothing at all.
lines.zh: 要嘛做一次超棒的運動，要嘛乾脆什麼都不做。

lines.en: And I've realized that showing up and doing a simple workout is what gives us energy to do even more.
lines.zh: 而我發現，願意開始、做一個簡單的運動，才是讓我們有能量做更多的關鍵。

lines.en: Step number five, the brain dump journal.
lines.zh: 第五步，腦袋清空日記。

lines.en: This is the step that changed the most for me personally.
lines.zh: 這是對我個人改變最大的一步。

lines.en: And it's the one I think most people underestimate. Journaling.
lines.zh: 也是我覺得大多數人最低估的一步：寫日記。

lines.en: But not in the way you probably think.
lines.zh: 但不是你想的那種。

lines.en: I'm not talking about keeping a diary.
lines.zh: 我不是說寫流水帳日記。

lines.en: I'm not talking about writing three pages of stream of consciousness every morning, although that's amazing.
lines.zh: 我也不是說每天早上寫三頁意識流的文字，雖然那也很棒。

lines.en: I'm talking about a specific structured 5-to-10-minute practice that is decades of peer-reviewed research behind it.
lines.zh: 我說的是一種有特定架構、5 到 10 分鐘的練習，背後有數十年同儕審查的研究支持。

lines.en: The foundational work comes from psychologist James Pennebaker at the University of Texas at Austin.
lines.zh: 這方面的基礎研究來自德州大學奧斯汀分校的心理學家 James Pennebaker。

lines.en: His research on what he called expressive writing demonstrated that writing about your thoughts and emotions,
lines.zh: 他對所謂「表達性書寫」的研究證明，寫下你的想法和情緒，

lines.en: particularly stressful ones, for as little as 15 to 20 minutes, produces measurable improvements in both mental and physical health.
lines.zh: 尤其是有壓力的那些，只要短短 15 到 20 分鐘，就能讓身心健康都有可測量的改善。

lines.en: We're talking about reduced blood pressure, improved liver function, stronger immune response, and fewer doctor visits from writing.
lines.zh: 我們說的是血壓降低、肝功能改善、免疫反應更強，還有因為寫作而少看醫生。

lines.en: Neuroimaging research from UCLA helps explain why.
lines.zh: UCLA 的腦部造影研究有助於解釋原因。

lines.en: Expressive writing activates the prefrontal cortex, your executive control center, while simultaneously dampening activity in the amygdala.
lines.zh: 表達性書寫會啟動前額葉皮質，也就是你的執行控制中心，同時抑制杏仁核的活動。

lines.en: So, the act of translating chaotic emotional experiences into structured language literally rebalances the relationship between your thinking brain and your fear brain. And it gets better.
lines.zh: 所以把混亂的情緒經驗轉化成有結構的語言，實際上是在重新平衡你的「思考腦」和「恐懼腦」之間的關係。而且還有更好的。

lines.en: Research has shown that regular journaling practice can reduce cortisol levels by up to 23% in consistent practitioners.
lines.zh: 研究顯示，持之以恆的人規律寫日記，皮質醇濃度最多可降低 23%。

lines.en: A study on people with major depressive disorder found significant improvements in depression scores after just 5 days of expressive writing.
lines.zh: 一項針對重度憂鬱症患者的研究發現，只做了 5 天表達性書寫，憂鬱分數就明顯改善。

lines.en: And a meta-analysis of 20 randomized controlled trials confirmed that journaling is an effective adjunct intervention for anxiety and PTSD.
lines.zh: 而一項綜合 20 個隨機對照試驗的統合分析證實，寫日記是治療焦慮和創傷後壓力症候群的有效輔助方法。

lines.en: Here's what I also find fascinating.
lines.zh: 還有一點我也覺得很有意思。

lines.en: A study published in the journal Mindfulness found that people who practice mindful journaling for just 10 minutes each morning showed greater self-control and were less likely to abandon their other habits throughout the day.
lines.zh: 發表在《Mindfulness》期刊的一項研究發現，每天早上只做 10 分鐘正念日記的人，自制力更強，一整天也比較不會放棄其他習慣。

lines.en: So, journaling doesn't just help you process emotions.
lines.zh: 所以寫日記不只幫你消化情緒。

lines.en: It strengthens the neural infrastructure for discipline itself.
lines.zh: 它還會強化自律本身的神經基礎。

lines.en: And I know what you're thinking, "Jay, what do I write about?
lines.zh: 我知道你在想：「Jay，我要寫什麼？

lines.en: Maybe I won't have anything to say.
lines.zh: 也許我根本沒東西可寫。

lines.en: Maybe I'll get lost or stuck."
lines.zh: 也許我會寫到迷失或卡住。」

lines.en: I found that even just trying to remember my dreams was an incredible place to start.
lines.zh: 我發現，光是試著回想自己的夢，就是很棒的起點。

lines.en: I remember just writing about how I felt in the morning, whether I was tired, upset, worried about something was just useful.
lines.zh: 我記得我只是寫下早上的感覺，是累、是難過，還是在擔心什麼，就很有用。

lines.en: It didn't have to be perfect.
lines.zh: 不必完美。

lines.en: It didn't have to be something that I'd have to hand in for an exam.
lines.zh: 也不必是要交出去考試的東西。

lines.en: And it's weird, isn't it, how we've all programmed ourselves to think like when you're writing it's like it's a test, it's an exam, it's going to be amazing.
lines.zh: 很奇怪對吧，我們都被設定成一寫東西就覺得像考試、像測驗，一定要寫得很棒。

lines.en: No one's ever going to read this. It's for you. Here's the practical step.
lines.zh: 沒有人會看這個，這是寫給你自己的。實際步驟是這樣。

lines.en: Every morning, spend 5 to 10 minutes writing by hand.
lines.zh: 每天早上花 5 到 10 分鐘手寫。

lines.en: And yes, by hand matters because handwriting engages different motor and cognitive circuits than typing. Answer three simple prompts.
lines.zh: 對，手寫很重要，因為手寫和打字動用的是不同的動作和認知迴路。回答三個簡單的問題。

lines.en: One, what am I genuinely grateful for today?
lines.zh: 一，今天我真心感謝的是什麼？

lines.en: Gratitude journaling has its own body of evidence for boosting positive effect and counteracting depressive thought patterns.
lines.zh: 感恩日記本身就有很多證據顯示能提升正面情緒、抵銷憂鬱的思考模式。

lines.en: Two, what's the single most important thing I need to accomplish today?
lines.zh: 二，今天我最需要完成的一件事是什麼？

lines.en: This forces prioritization and activates your prefrontal cortex for planning.
lines.zh: 這會逼你排定優先順序，並啟動前額葉皮質來做規劃。

lines.en: And three, what's one thought or worry I need to get out of my head?
lines.zh: 三，我需要把哪一個想法或擔憂從腦中清出來？

lines.en: This is the expressive writing piece.
lines.zh: 這就是表達性書寫的部分。

lines.en: You're externalizing intrusive thoughts so they stop consuming working memory.
lines.zh: 你是把侵入性的想法外化出來，讓它們不再占用工作記憶。

lines.en: You're literally freeing up cognitive bandwidth.
lines.zh: 你實際上是在釋放認知頻寬。

lines.en: Three questions, five minutes, the reset says it works.
lines.zh: 三個問題、五分鐘，研究顯示這個重置方法有效。

lines.en: Step six, delay the scroll. Protect your first hour.
lines.zh: 第六步，延後滑手機，守住你的第一個小時。

lines.en: This last step might be the simplest to understand and the hardest to actually do.
lines.zh: 這最後一步可能是最容易理解、卻最難真正做到的。

lines.en: And it might also be the most important.
lines.zh: 它可能也是最重要的。

lines.en: Do not check your phone, no email, no social media, no news for the first 60 minutes after waking up.
lines.zh: 起床後的頭 60 分鐘不要看手機，不看郵件、不看社群媒體、不看新聞。

lines.en: Here's why this matters so much from a neuroscience perspective.
lines.zh: 從神經科學的角度，這為什麼這麼重要？

lines.en: Remember that I mentioned your brain is in a highly programmable state in the first hour after waking?
lines.zh: 還記得我說過，起床後第一個小時大腦處在非常容易被設定的狀態嗎？

lines.en: The transition from sleep to full wakefulness involves a shift from theta and alpha brain waves to beta.
lines.zh: 從睡眠過渡到完全清醒，腦波會從 θ 波和 α 波轉換到 β 波。

lines.en: During that transition, your brain is exceptionally receptive to external input.
lines.zh: 在這段過渡期，你的大腦對外在訊息特別容易吸收。

lines.en: It's forming the emotional and cognitive framework for the entire day.
lines.zh: 它正在形成一整天的情緒和認知架構。

lines.en: When you immediately check your phone, you're doing something very specific to your neurochemistry.
lines.zh: 當你一醒來就看手機，你是在對大腦的神經化學做一件很特定的事。

lines.en: Every notification, every email, every social media post triggers microdoses of dopamine, the neurotransmitter associated with reward-seeking behavior.
lines.zh: 每一則通知、每一封郵件、每一篇社群貼文，都會觸發微量的多巴胺，也就是和追求獎勵行為有關的神經傳導物質。

lines.en: But it's not the satisfied content dopamine of accomplishment.
lines.zh: 但那不是完成一件事後滿足、安心的多巴胺。

lines.en: It's the restless craving dopamine of novelty seeking.
lines.zh: 而是追求新鮮感時那種躁動、渴求的多巴胺。

lines.en: You're training your brain in its most impressionable window to be reactive rather than intentional.
lines.zh: 你是在大腦最容易被影響的時段，訓練它變得被動反應，而不是主動有意識。

lines.en: Research has shown that checking email and social media first thing in the morning increases stress levels and fragments attention, reducing your ability to enter deep, focused work later.
lines.zh: 研究顯示，一早起來就看郵件和社群媒體，會提高壓力、分散注意力，降低你之後進入深度專注工作的能力。

lines.en: You're essentially letting other people's agendas, their emails, their posts, their news cycles set the emotional tone of your day before you've had a chance to set your own.
lines.zh: 你基本上是讓別人的議程，他們的郵件、貼文、新聞，在你有機會設定自己的基調之前，就決定了你一天的情緒基調。

lines.en: And there's a compounding effect.
lines.zh: 而且還有累加效應。

lines.en: Neuroscientist Andrew Huberman has talked extensively about the importance of staying within your own mental frame during the first hours of the day.
lines.zh: 神經科學家 Andrew Huberman 曾詳細談過，在一天的頭幾個小時留在自己的思考框架裡有多重要。

lines.en: When you pick up your phone, you're stepping out of your frame and into everyone else's.
lines.zh: 當你拿起手機，就是走出自己的框架，走進其他所有人的框架。

lines.en: The cognitive cost of switching back is real.
lines.zh: 切換回來的認知成本是真實存在的。

lines.en: It's called attention residue, and research shows it can impair your focus for the next task even after you've put the phone down.
lines.zh: 這叫「注意力殘留」，研究顯示，即使你已經放下手機，它還是會削弱你對下一項任務的專注。

lines.en: There's also a lesser-known benefit to delaying caffeine, which pairs well with this step.
lines.zh: 延後喝咖啡還有一個比較少人知道的好處，和這一步很搭。

lines.en: If you drink coffee too early, you interfere with that natural clearance process, and you're more likely to crash later.
lines.zh: 如果太早喝咖啡，會干擾身體自然的清除過程，之後更容易崩潰沒精神。

lines.en: Delaying your first cup by 60 to 90 minutes means the caffeine hits when your body actually needs it, and the effect lasts longer without a harsh drop-off.
lines.zh: 把第一杯延後 60 到 90 分鐘，咖啡因就會在身體真正需要時發揮作用，效果也更持久，不會突然大幅下滑。

lines.en: Here's the practical step. Put your phone in another room before bed.
lines.zh: 實際步驟是這樣：睡前把手機放到別的房間。

lines.en: Or at minimum, keep it face down with notifications silenced until you've completed steps one through five.
lines.zh: 或至少把它螢幕朝下、通知靜音，直到你完成第一到第五步。

lines.en: Use a cheap alarm clock instead of your phone alarm.
lines.zh: 用便宜的鬧鐘取代手機鬧鐘。

lines.en: If you need to ease into this, start by delaying your phone check by just 10 minutes, 20 minutes, 30 minutes, and build from there.
lines.zh: 如果需要慢慢適應，先從延後 10 分鐘看手機開始，再延到 20、30 分鐘，逐步增加。

lines.en: Replace the scrolling with your sunlight walk, your movement, your journaling.
lines.zh: 用曬太陽散步、活動身體、寫日記來取代滑手機。

lines.en: Fill the space with intention rather than reaction.
lines.zh: 用有意識的行動，而不是被動反應來填滿這段時間。

lines.en: And if you're a coffee drinker, experiment with waiting 60 to 90 minutes after waking before your first cup.
lines.zh: 如果你喝咖啡，試著在起床後等 60 到 90 分鐘再喝第一杯。

lines.en: I promise your afternoon self will thank you.
lines.zh: 我保證下午的你會感謝你。

lines.en: Thank you so much for listening.
lines.zh: 非常感謝你的收聽。

lines.en: I know that you might not be able to do all six of these steps starting tomorrow.
lines.zh: 我知道你可能沒辦法明天就把這六個步驟全部做到。

lines.en: I don't want you to.
lines.zh: 我也不希望你這樣做。

lines.en: Choose one that makes a difference and add one every week after you feel comfortable with the one you've implemented.
lines.zh: 先選一個會帶來改變的，等你對已經實行的那一個感到自在後，每週再加一個。

lines.en: I hope this transforms your morning.
lines.zh: 希望這能改變你的早晨。

lines.en: I hope it lets you retake back your time and your energy and I can't wait to see what you go on to create with this new found resilience.
lines.zh: 希望它能讓你奪回你的時間和精力，我很期待看到你帶著這份新的韌性去創造什麼。

lines.en: Thank you for listening. I'll see you soon.
lines.zh: 謝謝收聽，我們很快再見。

lines.en: Thank you so much for listening to this conversation.
lines.zh: 非常感謝你收聽這次的對話。

lines.en: If you enjoyed it, you'll love my chat with Adam Grant on why discomfort is the key to growth and the strategies for unlocking your hidden potential.
lines.zh: 如果你喜歡，你一定也會喜歡我和 Adam Grant 的對談，聊為什麼不適是成長的關鍵，以及釋放潛能的策略。

lines.en: If you know you want to be more and achieve more this year, go check it out right now.
lines.zh: 如果你知道自己今年想成為更好的人、達成更多目標，現在就去看看。

lines.en: You set a goal today, you achieve it in 6 months, and then by the time it happens, it's almost a relief.
lines.zh: 你今天設下一個目標，六個月後達成了，但到它真的發生時，幾乎只剩下鬆了一口氣的感覺。

lines.en: There's no sense of meaning and purpose.
lines.zh: 沒有意義感和目標感。

lines.en: You sort of expected it and you would have been disappointed if it didn't happen.
lines.zh: 你差不多預期它會發生，如果沒發生你還會失望。
